action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Issue #230 — a web control surface on the remote port: investigation notes
2	
3	Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/299903e5`, HEAD `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1), branch `dispatch/230-…`.
4	Read: CLAUDE.md (system-supplied copy), `docs/design.md` (remote status §3107, trust boundary §219), `docs/lessons.md`, `docs/remote-client.md` §§3–5, 10–13 (§4.1–4.4 read in full), `src/adapters/remote.rs` (1–560, 586–660, 765–880, 960–976), `src/app.rs` (remote regions), `src/core/remote.rs`, `src/ports/remote.rs` (1–150), `src/ui/remote.rs`, `control/src/lib.rs` (SessionView), `src/ui/cards.rs` (caption and excerpt), `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`, `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`, `tests/remote.rs` (names and helpers), `Cargo.toml`. Nothing was run and nothing was edited.
5	
6	## 1. The surface the page would sit on
7	
8	**Routing and responses.** `serve_remote` (`src/app.rs:3017`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/` prefix with a 404 JSON `not_found` (`src/app.rs:3023`). That refusal runs on the frame, so every stray `GET /` costs a frame pass and an unauthenticated slot. Only `GET /api/v1/info` and `POST /api/v1/pair` are answered before authentication (`src/app.rs:3028-3029`). `respond` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:530-553`) writes `Content-Type: application/json` unconditionally (line 545) and has no way to add headers. `RemoteReply` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:389-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}` with no headers field, so neither `Set-Cookie` nor a CSP can leave the port today.
9	
10	**Request parsing.** `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444`) keeps the query, the `Authorization: Bearer` value (line 487), and `Upgrade` with `Sec-WebSocket-Key` (line 491). It discards `Cookie`, `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-*`, `User-Agent` and `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. Nothing checks `Host`.
11	
12	**WebSocket.** `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) writes a 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. The upgrade's bearer check runs in `serve_remote` before `remote_subscribe` (`src/app.rs:3036-3037`, `authenticate` at `src/app.rs:3127`). A refused upgrade gets the JSON error as a plain HTTP response, which a browser's WebSocket object cannot read.
13	
14	**TLS.** `tls_config` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:144-155`) sets no ALPN, so a client falls back to HTTP/1.1. The certificate is made with `rcgen::CertificateParams::new(vec![])` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102`): no subject alternative names, a common name of `Switchboard <server_id>`, and rcgen's default far-future `not_after` (per the doc comment at line 91).
15	
16	**Pools and limits.** `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:567-568`). The accept loop drops a stranger past the pool at once (`src/adapters/remote.rs:701-706`). A connection starts in the unauthenticated pool and moves to the paired pool only on its first authenticated reply (`src/adapters/remote.rs:835-845`). After the first request the read timeout is `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30 s` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:573`), so a keep-alive connection holds its slot for up to 30 s after its last request. Rate windows cover only the exact paths `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`src/adapters/remote.rs:583-586`, `631-639`).
17	
18	**Pairing.** `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606`) checks the body's `spki_sha256` against the host's (`src/app.rs:3636`) before the code (`src/app.rs:3646`). A wrong key or a wrong code each count against the global window (`PairingFailed`). The success reply is a JSON body carrying the token in clear (`src/app.rs:3660-3665`), with `scope`, `server_id` and `device_id`. The token is stored only as its SHA-256 (`src/core/remote.rs:166` `new_device`). The window is single use (`src/core/remote.rs`, the `Paired` arm closes `self.pairing`). The device name is the body's `device_name`, trimmed to 64 characters, default `"Device"` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`, `src/core/remote.rs:166-174`).
19	
20	**Refusals and logs.** `refuse` (`src/app.rs:3754-3772`) logs method and path, not the query, so the `code` in `?code=` is not logged on a refusal. The `authenticate` refusals for a missing bearer and for an unknown token share the code `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`). The page therefore cannot tell "revoked" from "never paired" from the code.
21	
22	**Scope.** `GET /api/v1/info` (`src/app.rs:3568-3599`) returns identity, `capabilities` (line 3580), limits and `pairing_open`. It does not return the caller's scope, and no endpoint does. A read device sending a command gets 403 `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3173`). The only place a page could learn its scope is the pair reply body.
23	
24	**Send.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` takes `{op, text}` (`src/app.rs:3179`, `3192`), with `text` capped at `SEND_BYTES_CAP` (16 KiB) and `op` at 64 characters. Command routing is `remote_command` (`src/app.rs:3159`).
25	
26	**Pairing window UI.** `pairing` (`src/ui/remote.rs:141`) builds the QR payload at lines 160-165 as JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`. `addresses` holds the single result of `remote::local_address()` (`src/ui/remote.rs:157`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:962-969`, an IPv4 UDP-connect trick). The text form is the same JSON, copied by "Copy invite" (`src/ui/remote.rs:201-205`). The QR is a `qrcode` texture (`src/ui/remote.rs:280`).
27	
28	**A tree fact the QR does not reflect.** `bind_remote` listens on loopback unless `identity.listen.lan` is set (`src/app.rs:2962-2966`). The pairing window does not check that: it always prints `local_address()` (`src/ui/remote.rs:157`), so with LAN off the QR names an address the listener does not answer. The plan has to decide whether opening the window requires LAN.
29	
30	## 2. What is stored, and how the port rehydrates
31	
32	**On disk.**
33	- `identity.json`: `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26`) with `server_id`, `server_name`, the DER certificate, `spki_sha256`, `created`, `listen`. It has a `schema_version` field but the device file does not.
34	- The private key is a Keychain item under `remote-key:<server_id>` (`src/ports/remote.rs` `key_account`).
35	- `devices.json`: a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96`; `load_devices` returns the vec with `unwrap_or_default`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-82`). Fields: `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen` (`#[serde(default)]`). Adding a field needs `#[serde(default)]` on it; there is no version to bump.
36	- Session records, projects, sets and so on: the app's existing store. The port reads them through `AppCore` and never writes them.
37	
38	**What a browser device adds to disk.** One more `PairedDevice` row: a name, a scope, the token's hash, times. The token itself is never stored. The cookie or the header the browser keeps lives only in that browser. The name is the only new data; a user-agent-derived name would be a string the device supplies, trimmed and capped at 64 characters, as today.
39	
40	**Rehydration on the host.** On launch the core reads `identity.json` and `devices.json` (`IdentityLoaded`, `src/core/remote.rs`), and the port binds when the key is present (`bind_remote`). Session state comes back from the store in the usual `StoreLoaded` then `HostListed` reconcile. The port's epoch is per run, so a host restart changes `epoch` and every client refetches.
41	
42	**Rehydration in the page.** The page holds nothing that survives a visit except what it stores itself. The tree gives it no store:
43	- the token, if it is kept at all, lives where the decision in §3 puts it;
44	- the host's key, for an "identity changed, pair again" comparison on a later visit. Nothing in the tree stores a key for the page, and `/info` only gives the current one. A page reopened without a code therefore has no earlier key to compare against unless the plan stores it somewhere (localStorage, IndexedDB, or a cookie). The issue does not say where.
45	
46	So a reopened page rehydrates by `GET /api/v1/info`, then the reads it needs, then the events socket with subscribe-then-snapshot (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.4). The page's own state is UI state, not a read model (§12.6).
47	
48	## 3. What the pane shows, and what the tree lacks for it
49	
50	**The list.** `GET /api/v1/projects`, `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions`, `GET /api/v1/waiting` exist (`src/app.rs:3040-3060`). `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-678`) carries `kind`, `liveness`, `card` (a state word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `trust_question`, `name`, `project`, `last_stop_at_ms`, `quiet_secs` and `last_activity_ms`. Grouping by project, waiting first and marked, is possible with what is there.
51	
52	**The excerpt is not on the wire.** The issue asks for "the one-line excerpt the card shows". In the tree the card's excerpt is computed in the UI: for Claude Code sessions it is `agent_excerpt(conversation)` (`src/ui/cards.rs:558-574`), a function of the parsed transcript; for other kinds it is the caption or the host title (`src/ui/cards.rs:176-180`). `SessionView` has no excerpt field. `docs/remote-client.md` §4.4 and §4.3 name a `last_message` from the `Stop` hook as a metadata field, but `grep` finds no such field in `control/src/lib.rs` or the port. The excerpt would need either an additive wire field computed in the core (CLAUDE.md: logic under `ui/` moves to the core; `docs/lessons.md`, "Keep `ui.rs` dumb"), or one `last-response` fetch per Claude session.
53	
54	**The session view.** `GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/last-response` is served (`src/app.rs:1967`, routed at `src/app.rs:3101`), and `GET .../screen?lines=` is served by the same route family (`src/app.rs:1947`). A Claude session's response is `last-response`; anything else uses `screen`. Both are masked before they are cut (the redaction policy in `docs/remote-client.md` §4.3 and `remote_content_route`, `src/app.rs:1947-2024`).
55	
56	**The reply.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` (`src/app.rs:3179-3192`). The page can make `op` a UUID and send it again only on a timeout, which follows §4.5.
57	
58	**Live updates.** `changed {kind,id}` for `session`, `sessions`, `waiting`, `conversation` and `screen` are emitted by the read-model diff (`src/core/revision.rs`, which the file list in design.md names, and the port's events). A session that starts waiting therefore produces `changed {waiting}` and the page refetches the collection, as the issue asks.
59	
60	**The "device's scope" in the header.** The page can show the host name from `/info`. It cannot show the device's scope from any endpoint (see §1, Scope). If the plan keeps only a cookie, it needs an endpoint or a field for the caller's scope, or it has to store the scope from the pair reply and accept that a dialog change does not reach the page until a refusal.
61	
62	**"Revoked".** A revoked device gets `401 unauthorized` with "the token is not known; pair again" (`src/app.rs:3142-3148`), the same code as a device that never paired (`src/app.rs:3129-3135`). The page would need a distinct code. A revoked device's WebSocket is closed (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.5, and the `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket` test in `tests/remote.rs:2891`), and a browser WebSocket cannot read a refused upgrade's body (see Open questions).
63	
64	## 4. The pairing URL and the native text path
65	
66	- `PairingInvite` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`, the `parse` function at the end of the file) decodes JSON only (`Wire.decode`). A URL form needs a second parser on the Swift side, and the CLI's one-argument `pair` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`, the `pair` branch, `rest.count == 1`) calls it directly.
67	- `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:158-164` tests the JSON invite from an inline string, not from `client/Fixtures/`. No invite fixture exists in `client/Fixtures/` (its 28 files are reply bodies such as `pair.json` and `info.json`).
68	- `tests/remote.rs` drives the port with a raw TLS client (`http()`, `tests/remote.rs:245-297`, `Host: localhost`, pinned through `pinned_client`), and `pair()` (`tests/remote.rs:406`) posts `/pair` with the JSON body. The `crate::adapters` module is public (`src/lib.rs:19`), so a test can reach the page constants.
69	- The URL's `key` parameter matches `spki_sha256` in `/info` and the `/pair` body. Both are checked by the host already (`src/app.rs:3636`), so the page's own comparison adds a refusal before the code is sent, not a second trust check.
70	- The refusal logs carry method and path only (`src/app.rs:3754-3772`), so `?code=` is not written to the log by the port. Nothing else in the port logs a request line.
71	
72	## 5. Dependencies and rules the plan has to respect
73	
74	- `Cargo.toml` has `tungstenite 0.30`, `rustls` (ring), `rcgen`, `base64`, `qrcode` (no default features), `rustix`, `getrandom`, `sha2`, `uuid`, `serde_json`. No cookie or user-agent crate. A cookie parser or UA name mapping would be hand-written, or added as a dependency with a CI check.
75	- `web/` does not exist in the tree. The `include_str!` files and a route table would be new.
76	- CLAUDE.md: the `unsafe` ban and the Linux CI rule apply to any new code. The embedded page is not egui, so the UI-test rule in CLAUDE.md does not cover it; `tests/remote.rs` does.
77	- CLAUDE.md "Adding a feature" wants an action variant and core test, an effect for the outside world, and README and design.md updates. A static route is adapter-only, and a `CHANGELOG.md` line under Unreleased is required for a user-visible change.
78	- The trust-boundary paragraph in `docs/design.md` (around line 219-262) would need the page's sentence, as §5 of `docs/remote-client.md` already says.
79	- CLAUDE.md asks for a spike directory before building on a new risky mechanism. A browser's handling of a self-signed certificate, cookies and WebSockets on it is one, which is why it is listed below as a run-or-source question.
80	- Redaction is unaffected: the page reads through the same content routes. Static files carry no session data and do not need the redaction path.
81	
82	## 6. Which decisions the tree already settles, and which it leaves to the plan
83	
84	Settled by the tree (the plan should cite, not re-decide):
85	- Auth for every non-static read is the bearer, checked in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`), and the token is stored only as its hash (`src/core/remote.rs:166`).
86	- `/pair` already refuses a key that is not the host's (`src/app.rs:3636`) before the code is checked.
87	- A WebSocket subscription needs `Upgrade` and a bearer (`src/app.rs:3036-3037`, `src/app.rs:2723`).
88	- Pools: 4 unauthenticated, 12 paired, rate windows only on `/pair` and `/info`.
89	
90	Left to the plan (design choices, not open questions here): the cookie vs. subprotocol choice for the token; the click-through trust step; one QR or two; the static path table and headers; which pool a page load counts against; the device name's source; the excerpt field; the scope endpoint; the distinct revoked code; the LAN requirement for opening the pairing window; where the page keeps a pinned key.
91	
92	## 7. What I did not check
93	
94	- I did not run the host, the tests, or any browser. Nothing here is measured.
95	- I did not read `src/adapters/remote.rs` 560–765 and 880–1088 beyond their names (the subscriber loop, `serve`'s pools in detail, the tests), nor `src/app.rs` beyond the remote regions I listed, nor `src/core/revision.rs`, the watch set, the content cache, or the worker.
96	- I did not read the Swift transport (`SwitchboardTransport`), the pinning delegate, `client/Fixtures/*.json` contents, or the visionOS app.
97	- I did not read `spikes/22-remote-port` beyond its file list and the design's summary of its results.
98	- I did not confirm the event kinds from the diff code or the tests; `docs/design.md` and `tests/remote.rs` names say they exist.
99	- I did not check `scripts/bundle.sh`, the README's dev-aid list, or the CHANGELOG format.

101	## Open questions
102	
103	- [source] Whether Chrome, Safari on macOS, and Safari on iOS/iPadOS let a user click through the warning for a self-signed certificate with no subject alternative name, a common name only, and a far-future expiry, when the host is an IP address.

1	# Facts for #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run. The decisive question (Safari's `wss://` after a click-through) is settled in shape by sources, and its current behaviour needs an iPhone, so it goes to the owner. Questions about the tree are answered in the investigation and not repeated.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	1. **A browser `WebSocket` cannot set headers; its only handshake inputs are the URL and subprotocol names.** WHATWG: `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`, no options (https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/#the-websocket-interface). MDN agrees (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket/WebSocket). Query: "WebSocket constructor cannot set custom headers Authorization browser WHATWG Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token".
8	
9	2. **A subprotocol-carried token needs the 101 to echo an offered protocol.** WHATWG: a non-empty `protocols` with no acknowledging `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` fails the connection. RFC 6455 §4.2.2: the value must derive from the client's offer (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1). `respond_upgrade` writes none today and `read_request` drops the header (investigation §1).
10	
11	3. **A script sees nothing of a refused upgrade.** WHATWG: user agents "must not convey any failure information to scripts"; `close` has code 1006, `wasClean=false`. MDN: no documented `error` properties. So "revoked" must be learned from a `fetch` 401, and `unauthorized` needs a distinct code for revoked (`src/app.rs:3129-3148`). Query: "WebSocket error event no information on failed handshake status code browser security".
12	
13	4. **Browsers send `Origin` on every WebSocket handshake; checking it is the server's job.** RFC 6455 §4.1 ("MUST include ... if the request is coming from a browser client"), §4.2.2 ("If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere"; answer 403). `read_request` drops `Origin` today (investigation §1).
14	
15	5. **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265bis §1: "cookies for a given host are shared across all the ports on that host"; §4.1.3.2: "Ports are the only piece of the origin model that `__Host-` cookies continue to ignore" (https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html). The draft defers "same-site" to another spec, so `Strict` across ports is not stated there. GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh (https://github.com/Syslifters/sysreptor/security/advisories/GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh) reports `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-site WebSocket handshake with no Origin check. Consequence: a cookie token needs the `Origin` check from 4, and a custom header on `fetch` (forces a preflight the host does not answer). `SameSite` alone is not the defence. Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent with WebSocket handshake same-site cross-port Origin header check cross-site WebSocket hijacking".
16	
17	6. **"No token in a URL" is this repo's rule, not a standard's.** `docs/remote-client.md:312` and `:318`. RFC 6455 does not forbid it; OpenReplay and an Auth0 thread advise against it for log leakage (leads, not standards). The plan keeps the repo rule.
18	
19	7. **Chrome ignores the common name; a certificate with no SAN fails hostname matching for a bare IP.** Since Chrome 58 (2017), `ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`: "does not contain a Subject Alternative Name extension containing a domain name or IP address"; Advanced > "Proceed (unsafe)" still offered. Evidence is user and vendor reports (Graylog, NethServer, Atlassian, Netgate, Metric Insights); no source contradicts it, and the tree confirms the empty SAN list (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102`). Query: "Chrome self-signed certificate IP address no subjectAltName ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe". The plan adds the listen address as an IP SAN. A certificate regenerated on the same key keeps `spki_sha256`.
20	
21	8. **Safari's `wss://` does not honour a certificate click-through; this is the plan's main constraint.** WebKit bug 158345, open since 2016, last update July 2021 still NEW: WebSockets run on CFStream with no challenge callback, and a fix needs a rewrite on NSURLSession (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345; origin report bug 41419). Cockpit documents current behaviour: Safari's default WebSocket on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs does not support `wss` with self-signed certificates "even when they are manually marked as trusted"; the options are Apple's experimental "NSURLSession WebSocket" flag or a valid certificate (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, undated). A vendor article tested on Safari 15.6.1 says Keychain "Always trust" makes `wss` work. An iOS 26 beta 3 forum post reports the same error (seen in results, not opened). Queries: "Safari iOS self-signed certificate warning \"visit this website\" WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate"; "WebKit Safari WebSocket self-signed certificate exception not honored wss NSURLSession WebSocket fixed enabled by default Safari 15". Consequence, whatever the owner reports: REST polling is the floor; the socket is an upgrade. Trusting the certificate on the device (the issue's download route) is what gives Safari a socket.
22	
23	9. **CSP `connect-src 'self'` has not matched `wss:` in Safari.** WebKit bug 201591 (2019; a 2021 comment says unfixed in Safari 14); MDN notes `'self'` does not cover WebSocket schemes in all browsers; W3C CSP issue #7 is the spec history. Newer Safari is untested. Use `connect-src 'self' wss:` (the host name is not known at compile time). Query: "CSP connect-src 'self' websocket ws wss same origin Safari not matching 'self' bug CSP3".
24	
25	10. **iPadOS Safari sends a Mac user agent by default.** Apple developer forum thread 119186 and MacStories: since iPadOS 13 only Slide Over keeps the Mobile token; `navigator.maxTouchPoints` is 5 on iPad, 0 on a Mac. Data from 2019-2020. A name from the user agent cannot say "iPad"; the page can send `maxTouchPoints` with the name, or the name reads "Safari on Mac". Query: "iPadOS Safari user agent Macintosh desktop-class browsing iPad detection".
26	
27	11. **Chrome's Local Network Access prompt does not cover a page fetching its own LAN address, nor WebSockets.** The first milestone covers "public network to a local network or loopback"; local-to-local is planned later; WebSocket is a listed known gap; prompt "launching in Chrome 142" (https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access). Safari's rule was not found. Query: "Chrome Local Network Access permission prompt fetch private IP address from page served from local network same address".
28	
29	## Unresolved
30	
31	**U1. A `Secure; HttpOnly` cookie set from a click-through IP origin: stored and sent on `fetch`?** Query: "Chrome certificate exception \"Proceed to\" self-signed cookies Secure attribute stored IP address https secure context"; results covered the warning only. Build so both work: the host accepts the cookie and the bearer header, the page feature-tests. If favourable, the cookie is the default and the token stays out of script; if not, the page keeps the token in `localStorage` and sends the bearer, and the paired-devices dialog says so. The plan never waits on this.
32	
33	**U2. Chrome's click-through covering `wss://` and persisting across restarts.** Only a 2011 WebKit list thread says Chrome treats acceptance as valid for both. Build to the polling floor from 8; if favourable, Chrome gets live events.
34	
35	**U3. Any browser pinning an SPKI hash for page `fetch`/`WebSocket`.** No source found providing it, and no fetched source says none does. Plan on none: the `key` check compares against `/info`, which an impostor also serves, so word it as a guard against a stale or mistyped address, not authentication. If one exists, nothing is added.
36	
37	**U4. Connections per page load; unprompted `/favicon.ico` or `apple-touch-icon` requests.** Not found. Build to: serve `/favicon.ico` as a static path or a 204, and give static GETs a pool separate from the four unauthenticated slots that `/pair` and `/info` use.
38	
39	**U5. Browser retry when the host drops a connection past the pool (`src/adapters/remote.rs:701`).** Not found. Build to: the page retries with backoff and says "host busy".
40	
41	**U6. Whether `history.replaceState` clears the `?code=` URL from back-forward cache and session restore, and from the Referer.** Query: "history.replaceState remove query string Referer referrer-policy fragment safari back-forward cache session restore URL"; only how-to pages. Build to: serve `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, call `replaceState` first, keep the code single-use with the five-minute window, and say in the dialog that the code is in the camera app's history.
42	
43	**U7. `Sec-Fetch-Site` on WebSocket handshakes; secure-context status of an IP-literal https origin.** Not found. Nothing in the plan depends on either: the Origin check from 4 stands, and the page uses no secure-context-only API.
44	
45	## For the owner
46	
47	**O1. On an iPhone, does the Camera open the QR's https URL in Safari, and after the warning does the page load, and does the events socket open?** Favourable: the socket is used. Unfavourable (expected from 8): the page polls and the dialog describes trusting the certificate on the device for live updates. Works in both: REST polling first, socket as an upgrade.
48	
49	**O2. Is the address `local_address()` picks the one the phone reaches (several interfaces, a VPN)?** Favourable: one address in the URL. Unfavourable: the window lists the other interface addresses as text beside the URL. Works in both: the list.
50	
51	**O3. Is one click-through the only trust step acceptable for a `control`-scope phone?** Favourable: the dialog says so. Unfavourable: the plan adds the certificate download. Works in both: default a browser device to `read` scope, with the owner raising it in the pairing window.
52

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

524:## 13. Explicit design decisions
The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.

## 5. Security and pairing

A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.

## 6. Discovery and connection lifecycle

### 6.1 Discovery

- The host advertises `_switchboard._tcp` while listening on a LAN interface.

        "stage": "investigate",
        "text": "root #1 a
### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.
